Pedestrian Accident Statistics in Denver
Denver’s high volume of pedestrian activity comes with real risk. According to the most recent data available from the
Colorado Department of Transportation

, 591 pedestrians were killed on Colorado roads between 2021 and 2025, a 36 percent increase over the previous five-year period. In 2024, 78 pedestrian fatalities occurred in the dark, accounting for 65 percent of all pedestrian deaths that year, and 81 fatalities, or 68 percent, happened outside of a marked crosswalk.

Looking at the broader trend, October and November stand out as Colorado’s deadliest months for pedestrians over the past decade, together accounting for 21.5 percent of all pedestrian fatalities between 2015 and 2024, a pattern pointing to visibility and driver attentiveness as recurring failures behind the wheel.

These numbers are not abstract to the families who live through them. A crash that takes only seconds can mean months of medical treatment, missed paychecks, and a long road to recovery. Denver’s continued growth, combined with heavier commuter and freight traffic throughout the metro area, means the risk to pedestrians is unlikely to ease on its own. Certain areas of the city also carry a higher risk than others.
Dangerous Intersections and Roads for Pedestrians in Denver
Certain Denver corridors account for a disproportionate share of pedestrian crashes, and recognizing them helps explain why so many claims trace back to the same stretches of road.
Dangerous intersections include:
Federal Boulevard:

Carries some of the heaviest pedestrian crash rates in the city, particularly near its intersections with Alameda Avenue, Evans Avenue, and Mississippi Avenue, where wide lanes and long blocks between marked crossings leave little margin for error.
Colfax Avenue:

Sits within Denver’s designated high-injury network, where wide lanes, long distances between signalized crossings, and heavy mixed traffic create conditions that are structurally difficult for people on foot to navigate safely, especially near Broadway and Colorado Boulevard.
Beyond these corridors, several road-related factors raise pedestrian risk across the city:
Poorly Lit Streets:
Reduced visibility during evening and early morning hours contributes to a majority of fatal pedestrian crashes statewide.
Wide, High-Speed Arterials:
Roads designed to move vehicle traffic quickly often lack adequate pedestrian crossing infrastructure.
Limited Marked Crosswalks:
Long gaps between designated crossings push pedestrians toward unmarked crossings, where driver awareness is lower.
Heavy Commercial and Commuter Traffic:
Corridors serving both local business and through traffic see elevated conflict points between vehicles and pedestrians.

Common Injuries Sustained in Pedestrian Accidents

In a crash between a motor vehicle and a pedestrian, the vehicle almost always wins. The driver may walk away without a scratch, while the pedestrian may end up hospitalized with catastrophic harm. Being struck by a car can cause severe injury to nearly any part of the body, including the following:
Broken Bones
Contusions
Cuts, Scrapes, and Lacerations
Facial Injuries
Knee and Lower-Extremity Injuries
Loss of Limb
Organ Damage and Internal Bleeding
Rib Fractures and Chest Injuries
Road Rash
Scarring or Disfigurement
Skull Fractures
Soft-Tissue Injuries
Spinal Cord Injuries and Paralysis
Traumatic Brain Injuries

A pedestrian often suffers injuries in stages during a single collision: the initial impact with the bumper or hood, a second impact between the head or chest and the windshield as the body folds forward, and a third impact when the pedestrian lands in the road. This layered sequence is why a
Denver pedestrian accident lawyer
looks closely at the full scope of harm rather than treating a crash as a single point of injury.
Common Causes of Pedestrian Accidents

These layered injuries are rarely the result of chance. Driver error remains the leading cause of pedestrian collisions in Denver and across Colorado. Motorists frequently overestimate their own attentiveness, attempt to multitask while driving, or disregard traffic laws altogether, and pedestrians absorb the consequences of those mistakes.
The most common causes of pedestrian accidents in Denver include the following:
Distracted Driving or Improper Lookout
Texting and Driving
Operating Under the Influence of Drugs or Alcohol
Speeding, Especially in Residential or School Zones
Running a Red Light or Stop Sign
Failing to Yield the Right-of-Way to Pedestrians
Making Illegal Turns
Passing a Vehicle Stopped at a Crosswalk

Most of these behaviors are preventable when drivers stay alert and follow Colorado’s roadway rules, and while poor crosswalk design or pedestrian error can also play a role, fault in these cases usually falls on the driver, an imbalance that Colorado law reflects directly.
Colorado State Laws Protecting Pedestrians

Pedestrian safety in Colorado rests on a combination of state statutes and municipal codes that define how drivers and pedestrians must behave when their paths cross. Both groups carry legal duties, though pedestrians remain the more vulnerable party in nearly every interaction, which is why their rights receive close attention under state law.
Pedestrian Rights
Under
Colorado Revised Statutes § 42-4-802

, drivers must yield to pedestrians crossing within a marked or unmarked crosswalk, slowing or stopping as needed. Pedestrians in Denver and across the state carry several specific protections, including the following:
The right-of-way at both marked and unmarked crosswalks
Extra caution from drivers turning at intersections
Full crossing time when a walk signal is displayed
A complete stop from drivers at flashing red lights and stop signs when pedestrians are present
Heightened driver alertness near schools, neighborhoods, and high-foot-traffic areas
These protections form the legal baseline that drivers are expected to meet in every interaction with a pedestrian.
Pedestrian Responsibilities
Pedestrians also carry responsibilities of their own, and following them both supports safety and preserves the strength of a future injury claim. Pedestrians in Colorado are expected to:
Obey pedestrian traffic signals, including “walk” and “do not walk” indicators
Cross only at designated intersections or marked crosswalks when one is available
Pause at the curb to assess traffic before entering the roadway
Scan all directions, including behind, for approaching or turning vehicles
Enter the crosswalk only when it is clearly safe to do so
Avoid distractions such as phone use while crossing
Meeting these responsibilities strengthens a pedestrian’s position if a crash later leads to a legal claim.
Driver Responsibilities
Drivers carry the heavier share of the legal duty. Motorists must:
Yield to pedestrians crossing at intersections and marked crosswalks
Comply with every traffic and pedestrian control signal without exception
Stay alert for pedestrians near roadways, particularly when turning or approaching an intersection
Failing to meet these duties can create significant legal exposure once a crash occurs.
Who Can Be Held Liable?

Determining liability for a pedestrian accident starts with the state’s fault law. Colorado follows a fault-based system, meaning the person who caused the collision is responsible for paying for the resulting injuries and losses, rather than each party turning to their own insurer regardless of fault.
Depending on the facts of the crash, liability for a pedestrian accident could fall on:
The driver who struck you
The City of Denver
A property owner
A combination of these parties
Colorado also follows a modified comparative negligence framework under
Colorado Revised Statutes § 13-21-111

. An injured pedestrian can still recover damages as long as their share of fault is 50 percent or less, though any compensation awarded is reduced in proportion to that share, and a fault share above 50 percent bars recovery entirely. Exactly which party bears responsibility, and to what degree, depends on the specific facts of the crash, which is why a
Denver pedestrian accident lawyer
typically investigates the scene, gathers evidence, and identifies every liable party before a claim is filed.
Who Else Might Be Liable?

In some cases, a hazard contributes to a crash without a driver being directly at fault, such as a sidewalk defect, a missing pedestrian crossing, or a malfunctioning traffic signal. When one of these conditions plays a role, the State of Colorado or another government agency may be liable for failing to maintain safe road conditions.
Our team at
Dormer Harpring
conducts a comprehensive investigation into every accident we take on, and depending on what that investigation uncovers, liability may also extend to:
A driver’s employer, if the driver was working at the time of the crash
The manufacturer of a defective vehicle part
The agency responsible for road design
Another third party entirely
A thorough investigation into every possible source of liability often makes the difference in the final value of a claim.
What Compensation Can You Recover After a Pedestrian Accident?

Because pedestrians have no structural protection between their bodies and an oncoming vehicle, the resulting injuries tend to be severe, and the compensation available typically reflects that severity.
Recoverable damages may include:
Medical expenses, including emergency treatment, hospitalization, and ongoing rehabilitation
Lost wages and reduced earning capacity when an injury limits a person’s ability to work long-term
Future medical costs for serious injury cases requiring care well past the initial hospital stay
Pain and suffering tied to the physical and emotional impact of the injury
Emotional distress connected to the crash and its aftermath
Loss of enjoyment of life and a reduced ability to participate in activities enjoyed before the injury
Scarring or disfigurement resulting from the crash
Punitive damages in cases involving particularly reckless conduct

None of this compensation arrives automatically. The value of a claim depends heavily on how well each of these losses is documented from the start, and on whether every category of harm, not just the most obvious medical bills, is accounted for before a settlement is reached.
What to Do After a Pedestrian Accident in Denver

The actions taken immediately after a pedestrian accident can shape the strength of the resulting claim. Evidence disappears quickly, memories fade, and insurance companies begin building their version of events almost right away.
The following steps can help protect both your health and your claim:
Seek medical attention immediately, even if you feel fine, since some injuries do not show symptoms right away
Call law enforcement to the scene so an official report is created, or
file a crash report online
if an officer was not present
Photograph the scene, your visible injuries, and any relevant road conditions before anything is cleared or repaired
Collect names and contact information from any witnesses at the scene before they leave the area
Avoid giving a detailed statement to the insurance company before speaking with an attorney about your case
Contact a
Denver pedestrian accident lawyer
promptly so evidence can be identified and preserved while it still exists
A prompt, well-documented response gives your attorney more to work with when negotiations or litigation begin, and it limits the opportunities an insurance company has to dispute what happened.
How Long Do You Have to File a Pedestrian Accident Claim in Colorado?
These steps help preserve a claim in the short term, but a separate legal deadline governs whether that claim can be filed at all. Under
Colorado Revised Statutes § 13-80-101
, you must generally file personal injury claims arising from a motor vehicle collision, including pedestrian accidents, within three years from the date of the crash.

However, a handful of circumstances can affect that deadline. Claims against a government entity, such as the City of Denver, require a formal notice of claim within a much shorter window than the standard filing period, and the three-year period may pause in limited situations, such as when the injured person is a minor or when the cause of the injury was not reasonably discoverable right away. These exceptions are narrow and should never be assumed without legal guidance, since applying them incorrectly can cost an otherwise valid claim its filing window.
Pedestrian Safety Tips

The best outcome is still avoiding a crash in the first place. While you cannot control drivers’ actions, staying alert while walking or jogging in Denver and across Colorado can help reduce your risk. A few practical habits make a difference:
Make Yourself Visible:
Wear brightly colored or reflective clothing, make eye contact with drivers before crossing, and carry a light source if you must walk at night.
Stay Alert:
Assume drivers around you may not be paying attention, avoid looking at your phone while walking, and watch what nearby vehicles are doing before you cross.
Check Twice for Traffic:
Look both directions before crossing, even when you have the right-of-way, since drivers in Colorado do run red lights and roll through stop signs.

Even the most cautious pedestrian can still become the victim of a negligent or reckless driver. If you have been hit by a car in Denver, you have rights, and understanding them is the first step toward recovery.

faqs.question: Can I recover compensation if I was partially at fault?

children.text: Yes, as long as your share of fault is 50 percent or less. Your compensation is reduced based on your percentage of fault, but if you are more than 50 percent at fault, you cannot recover anything.

faqs.question: What if the driver fled the scene?

children.text: You may still recover compensation through your own insurance policy. Uninsured motorist coverage often applies when a driver flees the scene and cannot be identified, and Colorado insurers are required to offer this coverage as part of a standard auto policy. Reporting the crash to law enforcement right away improves the chances of identifying the driver later.

faqs.question: How much is my pedestrian accident case worth?

children.text: The value depends on the severity of your injuries, your medical costs, and how clearly fault can be established. More severe injuries generally involve higher medical expenses and higher lost income, both of which factor into the total value of a claim. A
Denver pedestrian accident lawyer
can review the specifics of your case to give you a clearer picture of what it may be worth.

faqs.question: How long do pedestrian accident claims take?

children.text: Most claims resolve within several months to a year, though serious injury cases can take longer. Cases with clear fault and stable injuries tend to move faster, while disputed liability or catastrophic injuries often require additional time to reach a fair resolution.
